ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> One hundred and ninety participants were recruited from Prolific Academic, where only participants with an approval rating of 90% or higher were eligible.

> Due to technical issues, data from two participants were not recorded correctly and were not included in the analyses.

> In Phase 1, participants were directed to complete the survey by describing themselves as they currently are and in relation to people with similar demographic characteristics (standard instructions from the IPIP website - https://ipip.ori.org/New_IPIP-50-item-scale.html).

> In Phase 2, participants were randomly allocated to one of three conditions; extreme (n = 55), midpoint (n = 68) or neutral (n = 65).

> All participants were instructed to complete the IPIP survey a second time, but this time on behalf of a hypothetical friend.

> Participants were told that this friend shares all the same interests and personality traits as they do, but participants in the extreme and midpoint conditions were additionally told that their friend usually responds to survey tasks by choosing the most extreme or midpoint response options, respectively.

> Since participants often ignore task instructions (Barnard et al., 1979), an attention check similar to that suggested by Oppenheimer et al. (2009) was also included to ensure participants had read the instructions completely.

> Participants were unable to begin the Phase 2 survey until they could successfully demonstrate they had read the instructions.

> At the completion of Phase 2, participants were again presented with the manipulation instruction and asked to indicate on a slider scale (ranging from 0 to 100) the degree to which they used these instructions to guide their responses.

> The first version, which we present here, was performed on a cleaned data set where participants were removed from the analysis if they failed two or more (of four possible) attention checks while completing the survey.

> Eleven participants were removed from the midpoint condition and two from the extreme condition due to these failed attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 175 participants.

> Given that participants were essentially instructed to overuse (extreme responding) or underuse (midpoint) the tail response options, the LASARS model predicts that these observed effects should all be accounted for by changes in the centre preference parameter.

> When participants were instructed to respond more extremely, their Phase 2 centre preference estimates were lower than their Phase 1 estimates, while those who were instructed to use the midpoint had notably higher centre preference parameters in Phase 2 compared to Phase 1.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: One hundred and ninety participants were recruited from Prolific Academic, where only participants with an approval rating of 90% or higher were eligible.
Due to technical issues, data from two participants were not recorded correctly and were not included in the analyses.

In Phase 1, participants were directed to complete the survey by describing themselves as they currently are and in relation to people with similar demographic characteristics (standard instructions from the IPIP website - https://ipip.ori.org/New_IPIP-50-item-scale.html).
In Phase 2, participants were randomly allocated to one of three conditions; extreme (n = 55), midpoint (n = 68) or neutral (n = 65).
All participants were instructed to complete the IPIP survey a second time, but this time on behalf of a hypothetical friend.

Participants were told that this friend shares all the same interests and personality traits as they do, but participants in the extreme and midpoint conditions were additionally told that their friend usually responds to survey tasks by choosing the most extreme or midpoint response options, respectively.

Since participants often ignore task instructions (Barnard et al., 1979), an attention check similar to that suggested by Oppenheimer et al. (2009) was also included to ensure participants had read the instructions completely.
Participants were unable to begin the Phase 2 survey until they could successfully demonstrate they had read the instructions.

At the completion of Phase 2, participants were again presented with the manipulation instruction and asked to indicate on a slider scale (ranging from 0 to 100) the degree to which they used these instructions to guide their responses.

The first version, which we present here, was performed on a cleaned data set where participants were removed from the analysis if they failed two or more (of four possible) attention checks while completing the survey.
Eleven participants were removed from the midpoint condition and two from the extreme condition due to these failed attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 175 participants.

Given that participants were essentially instructed to overuse (extreme responding) or underuse (midpoint) the tail response options, the LASARS model predicts that these observed effects should all be accounted for by changes in the centre preference parameter.

When participants were instructed to respond more extremely, their Phase 2 centre preference estimates were lower than their Phase 1 estimates, while those who were instructed to use the midpoint had notably higher centre preference parameters in Phase 2 compared to Phase 1.

text.text: All authors were involved in the conceptualisation of this work and the methodological and theoretical developments.
JKG curated the data and performed formal analysis, validation and visualisation with supervision and consultation from GEH, SDB and QFG.
JKG wrote the original draft and all authors were involved with review and editing.
A central goal of psychological research is the measurement and interpretation of individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and attitudes.
This task is inherently challenging because these phenomena are internal states that cannot be directly observed (Kim et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This task is inherently challenging because these phenomena are internal states that cannot be directly observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Kim et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Although these internal states may, at times, manifest in observable behaviours -for example, sadness may lead to crying -this relationship is neither consistent nor specific.
Not all sadness leads to crying, and not all crying comes from sadness.

Since observable behaviour provides such an incomplete representation of internal psychological states, detailed theories have been developed to help link behaviour with unobservable psychological processes, attitudes, and emotions (hereafter referred to broadly as "latent states").

One of the most widely used approaches for this purpose is self-report measurement, including open-ended questions, forced-choice tasks, Likert-type rating scales, and visual analogue scales, which are used extensively across psychology and related disciplines to assess individual differences in latent states.
However, before these states can be observed and analysed, they must be translated into a response, such as selecting an option on a Likert scale.

Understanding this translation process is therefore essential for interpreting self-report data and ensuring that observed responses provide valid information about individual differences in the constructs of interest.
In this paper, we propose a theoretical account of self-report responding in which observed responses arise from two separable but psychologically meaningful sources of individual differences.

Specifically, self-reported responses reflect both the latent states individuals intend to communicate and the response processes that govern how those states are translated into observable responses.

Although these response processes may be influenced by contextual factors, such as who is asking or the perceived consequences of responding, our framework proposes that individuals typically exhibit characteristic and relatively stable patterns of responding across measurement contexts.
These patterns reflect systematic individual differences in how internal experiences are mapped onto available response options.
As a result, observed self-report scores contain information not only about the latent states being assessed but also about stable differences in the response strategies individuals employ.
Understanding and distinguishing these two sources of variation is critical for the accurate measurement and interpretation of individual differences.

Though our theory can, in principle, be applied to any form of self-report, we focus here on Likert scale surveys because they are ubiquitous in psychological science (and beyond; Joshi et al., 2015).

text.text: Likert responses also provide a tractable setting in which to study systematic individual differences in response behaviour and to quantify how response styles contribute to variation in observed scores.

A typical Likert scale presents respondents with a series of statements or questions (called "items") and asks them to respond using an ordered set of "response options" (Batterton & Hale, 2017; Joshi et al., 2015; Likert, 1932).

Each response option represents an ordered category rather than a precise numerical quantity, allowing respondents to express gradations of opinion or experience in a structured and interpretable way.

This structured format makes them an excellent method for quickly, easily and affordably collecting data (Dillman et al., 2014) that is easy to analyse (Joshi et al., 2015) and may otherwise be difficult to obtain (Kim et al., 2008).

text.text: In this paper, we present a theoretical account of self-report response style that advances the measurement and interpretation of individual differences.

We conceptualise self-report response style as stable, multidimensional individual differences comprising distinct and psychologically interpretable processes that interact to produce a wide range of response patterns.
This framework treats response styles not merely as sources of measurement noise, but as meaningful and informative characteristics of individuals that systematically influence observed scores.

By representing response styles within a unified parametric framework, our theory provides a means of quantifying individual differences in response behaviour and generating testable predictions regarding their structure, stability, and influence on psychological measurement.
In doing so, it offers a principled approach for distinguishing substantive variation in latent states from variation attributable to how individuals communicate those states through self-report.

As in J. Grimmond et al. (2025), the modelling approach presented in this paper formalises our proposed theory and describes responses as arising from the interaction between a respondent's latent state and a decision process.
text.formatted: As in J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Grimmond et al. (2025)</ref>, the modelling approach presented in this paper formalises our proposed theory and describes responses as arising from the interaction between a respondent's latent state and a decision process.

text.text: In this ordinal-probit approach, each latent state is represented as a continuous, normal distribution characterised by a mean parameter (µ), reflecting the individual's level of endorsement of the construct of interest.
For example, µ might represent the true, latent level of stress which a self-report measure aims to assess.

When responding to a self-report item, a value is sampled from this latent distribution and mapped onto discrete response options via a set of ordered thresholds that partition the continuum into ordinal categories.

These thresholds capture how individuals use the response scale, effectively encoding response style, such that differences in their placement can produce different observed response patterns, even when latent states are identical (see J. Grimmond et al. (2025) for examples).

text.text: The theoretical account we propose here shifts the explanation of response style from the decision thresholds to underlying parameters which are directly interpretable at the psychological level; three parameters which govern the overall spacing, shift, and compression of the thresholds.
Shifting focus like this allows us to develop and test psychological theory about the relative stability vs. manipulability of response styles in a way previously not possible.

text.text: With this theoretical and empirical support, we propose the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, which defines three parameters that provide intuitive links between psychological theory and observed behaviour, reflecting the preference for centre options, directional bias and psychological collapsing in survey responding.
We label these parameters "centre preference" (α), "directional preference" (ω) and "odds preference" (γ), respectively.
The centre preference parameter reflects the degree to which people choose (or not) the middle response options on the Likert scale.

Larger values of the centre preference parameter indicate greater distance between the decision thresholds, increasing the likelihood of using middle options and decreasing the likelihood of using extreme response options.

The directional preference parameter captures asymmetry in response option selection, with larger values shifting the distribution of responses up toward the right-end options (often, but not always, toward agreement options) and away from left-end options.
Finally, the odds preference parameter reflects the use of end-plus-middle options, with the distance between the inner thresholds changing as a function of the outer, fixed thresholds.

Though this parameter is mathematically generalisable to scales with more than five response options, the interpretation varies with different numbers of options (we return to this point in the Discussion).

Given that 5-point scales are the most popular response format in survey research (Kusmaryono et al., 2022), we have labelled this parameter "odds preference" to describe how response patterns are affected by different values of this parameter in a 5-point format.

For the rest of this paper, we provide empirical tests of the proposed framework.
These studies evaluate predictions arising from the interpretation of response styles as meaningful individual differences in self-report responding.

We first demonstrate that response style is under conscious control and that different psychological dimensions can be selectively influenced by task demands without corresponding change in latent state scores.
We then show that, in the absence of explicit instructions to the contrary, individuals exhibit remarkably stable response styles across time and tasks.

Establishing response style stability in this way provides support for the theoretical assumption that response style can be shared across latent states to improve measurement and that response style constitutes a meaningful individual difference in its own right.
To conclude the paper, we identify and evaluate a novel theoretical prediction about response style expression in instruments with no reverse-coding within latent state scales.
Specifically, we confirm that a scale with no reverse-scoring within each latent state conflates directional bias (in this case, acquiescence) with latent state expression.

We show this occurs with conventional, model-free scoring techniques, but that the LASARS model offers a solution to this problem by leveraging response style information across tasks to reduce the potentially confounding effects of response style.

Together, the analyses in this paper provide a body of evidence that supports our proposed theory; decision styles and latent states are two distinct sources of information that can be separately but simultaneously measured to improve the fidelity and informativeness of survey measures.

The LASARS framework casts response styles as a decision process which can, theoretically, be manipulated independently of latent state expression (which is generally considered to be stable in individual differences research; John et al., 2010).

text.text: The IPIP measures the Big Five personality traits -extraversion, openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, and neuroticism.
Each trait is measured with 10 items and responses given on a 5-point Likert scale with response options labelled "Disagree" (1), "Neutral" (3), and "Agree" (5).
We also added two attention check items instructing participants to select a specific response option, resulting in a 52-item survey.

In Phase 1, participants were directed to complete the survey by describing themselves as they currently are and in relation to people with similar demographic characteristics (standard instructions from the IPIP website - https://ipip.ori.org/New_IPIP-50-item-scale.html).

In Phase 2, participants were randomly allocated to one of three conditions; extreme (n = 55), midpoint (n = 68) or neutral (n = 65).
All participants were instructed to complete the IPIP survey a second time, but this time on behalf of a hypothetical friend.

Since many people may not be consciously aware of their own survey responding styles/preferences, it was important that participants responded on behalf of somebody else in Phase 2, so response style could be more easily separated from personality constructs.

Participants were told that this friend shares all the same interests and personality traits as they do, but participants in the extreme and midpoint conditions were additionally told that their friend usually responds to survey tasks by choosing the most extreme or midpoint response options, respectively.
Participants in the neutral condition were not given any information about how their friend may respond and, in this way, served as a control group.
The full task instructions for each condition can be found in the Supplementary Material.

Since participants often ignore task instructions (Barnard et al., 1979), an attention check similar to that suggested by Oppenheimer et al. (2009) was also included to ensure participants had read the instructions completely.

At the completion of Phase 2, participants were again presented with the manipulation instruction and asked to indicate on a slider scale (ranging from 0 to 100) the degree to which they used these instructions to guide their responses.
Both phases were completed in the same session, with an overall median completion time of 10 minutes and 27 seconds.
Parameters were estimated separately for the Phase 1 and Phase 2 surveys.
That is, for each participant, we estimated separate latent state means for the five personality traits in Phase 1 and Phase 2, and three response style parameters in Phase 1 and Phase 2.
This resulted in a total of 16 parameters estimated per participant.

We used the Particle Metropolis within Gibbs (PMwG) sampling approach (Cooper et al., 2024; Gunawan et al., 2020; Kuhne et al., 2026) to estimate the Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters simultaneously, which has the advantage of providing covariance information about all pairwise combinations of the 16 parameters, allowing us to explore this in a principled, Bayesian way.

text.text: We estimated the model independently for each manipulation condition (extreme, midpoint and neutral).
The PMwG settings were the same for each of the three conditions' joint models.
Each model sampled 3000 iterations of 75 particles in the "burn-in" and "adaptation" phase and 50 in the "sampling" phase.
We used uninformative prior settings, whereby the prior for all 16 parameters was zero.
Two versions of the analyses were run.

The first version, which we present here, was performed on a cleaned data set where participants were removed from the analysis if they failed two or more (of four possible) attention checks while completing the survey.
They were also removed if their self-reported adherence to the instructions was less than 50/100 or if they failed to read the manipulation instructions correctly more than once.
Eleven participants were removed from the midpoint condition and two from the extreme condition due to these failed attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 175 participants.

A comparative analysis was performed on the full sample of 188 participants (results in Supplementary Material) to confirm that the model generates the same pattern of results when strict attention checks are not included.
There were no notable differences in the patterns observed between the two versions, so we report the results of the cleaned sample for simplicity.
For inference, we took the difference of group-level posterior distributions, and summarised the difference distribution by its posterior mean and 95% credible interval.

The centre preference parameter reflects the distance between the thresholds demarcating each response option on the latent scale.

text.text: Hence, we conclude that the selective influence of response style was successful for the most part; our manipulation resulted in no meaningful change among latent state estimates, while large differences were observed between Phase 1 and Phase 2 response style parameters, especially centre preference, as hypothesised.
Having established that response style can be influenced by conscious decision processes, it is also important to consider how such tendencies manifest in the absence of explicit manipulation.
In typical survey contexts, respondents are rarely instructed to adopt particular response strategies and instead rely on their default or habitual approaches to answer questions.

Establishing that these tendencies remain consistent over time is an important step in theory validation, as our proposed framework considers response style to be a meaningful source of individual difference rather than a purely situational factor.

If response styles are shown to persist across measurement occasions, our theory's prediction that they capture enduring decision-making preferences which systematically shape how individuals engage with rating scales will have empirical support.

text.text: As predicted by the theory, response style parameters show consistently strong temporal correlations, indicating that response styles are relatively stable over time.

Interestingly, the Time 1 and Time 2 estimates for all three response style parameters are more strongly related to one another than all but one of the latent state estimates across measurement occasions (excitement seeking).

text.text: Given that test-retest correlations are among the most widely used indicators of measurement reliability, this result has important implications for establishing temporal stability in individual differences research.
Accordingly, the reliability of self-report measures (when improvement is theoretically appropriate) is improved when viewed through the lens of our psychological theory.
In addition to temporal stability, response tendencies should generalise across instruments if they are stable individual differences as the LASARS model proposes.
However, the extent of this generalisation requires exploration because it may be attenuated by individuals' capacity to adapt their response strategies to align with specific task demands.
It is plausible that the observed temporal findings reflect consistent task demands that implicitly encourage particular response strategies across repeated administrations.
Indeed, the earlier results showing that task instructions can systematically alter response behaviour highlight the sensitivity of response styles to contextual cues.

As such, demonstrating cross-survey consistency is necessary to rule out the possibility that observed stability is merely a by-product of shared task structure and establish the true consistency of response style behaviour.

Confirming that response styles persist across measures that differ in response format, item content, and theoretical framing in this way provides stronger evidence that they reflect stable, trait-like individual differences rather than context-dependent side effects of specific survey designs.

Establishing the stability of response styles across tasks also represents an important step in validating the LASARS framework's assumption that individuals exhibit consistent response styles across latent states; the model leverages information from multiple latent constructs to identify patterns of consistency, thereby enabling the separation of response style effects from genuine latent state expression.

This assumption is supported by prior empirical work (Bolt & Newton, 2011; Wetzel et al., 2013), but it is not universally adopted in response style modelling approaches, many of which conceptualise response styles as varying at the item or trait level rather than as stable person-level tendencies (Böckenholt, 2017; Bolt & Newton, 2011).

In this analysis, we explore how response styles and latent states relate to one another across instruments with differential construct overlap and response formats.

Because each survey instrument aims to measure the same conceptual domain (impulsivity), we expect to find consistent relationships between latent state scores, but the LASARS model additionally predicts that people will adopt similar response strategies for the three different surveys because they have innate preferences for how they communicate self-report information.

In this way, LASARS suggests that, even with different response formats and wording, like-for-like response style parameters will be correlated across the three survey instruments because people's preferences for/against certain response options are consistent.

While the NEO and BIS11 are both relatively explicit measures of impulsive tendency that measure similar aspects of the trait, such as poor self-control, rash behaviour and lack of forethought, they differ on how they elicit the information.
The NEO's 5-point scale provides statements about impulsive behaviours (e.g., "I often do things on the spur of the moment") and asks people to rate their agreement.

The BIS11, while also adopting a 5-point scale and similar items (e.g., "I do things without thinking"), requires people to rate how regularly they engage in these behaviours on a scale from "Always" to "Never".
In this way, the two instruments may elicit different response behaviour because people conceptualise agreement and frequency differently.

The BIS-BAS measure differs not only in response option labelling (as with the NEO and BIS11) but also in response format altogether, employing a 4-point rather than a 5-point scale and omitting a neutral option.

It also approaches the construct definition differently, approaching impulsivity indirectly through motivational sensitivity to reward and approach cues rather than through failures of self-control or deliberation per se.

By simultaneously varying construct operationalisation, item framing, and response format, these surveys place a stronger test on the assumption that response styles reflect stable individual differences rather than task-specific behaviours.

The BIS11 and NEO odds preference parameters show a more moderate, but still substantial (r = .43), association, likely reflecting differences in response option labels.
Both instruments use 5-point scales, but the NEO asks respondents to indicate their degree of agreement, whereas the BIS11 asks how frequently people engage in the described behaviour.
These conceptual differences in response framing likely encourage distinct interpretations of scale use across tasks, reflected in different degrees of psychological collapse.

Despite these framing differences, the correlation between the two odds preference parameters remains stronger than all but one between-instrument latent state correlations (the exception being BIS11's motor impulsiveness and BIS-BAS fun-seeking scales which have a correlation coefficient of .61).
This provides strong evidence that response style is at least as stable (in most cases more stable) than the conceptually related latent state parameters.

This provides further evidence that response styles represent a robust, task-agnostic source of individual differences, persisting even when constructs are only loosely related and highlighting the importance of explicitly modelling response styles.
One other interesting response style relationship is between the odds preference and centre preference parameters within the BIS11, which are negatively correlated.

This pattern is theoretically interpretable because smaller odds preference estimates reflect a tendency toward even-category responding (i.e., responses of 2 and 4), which approximates midpoint responding (albeit with the loss of the neutral option), which would result in larger centre preference.

Although these response tendencies are not strict opposites, particularly given their differing implications for the unobserved midpoint response, they do reflect partially competing behaviours, accounting for the observed negative relationship.
Additional links between response styles and latent state parameters further support the proposed model's theory.
The NEO directional preference parameter shows relatively strong correlations with the BIS11 latent state parameters.

Because BIS11 subscales are entirely positively or negatively keyed, any systematic directional responding must necessarily be absorbed into the location of the latent state distribution rather than being captured explicitly by a directional shift in thresholds.

Importantly, the direction of these relationships is theoretically coherent; when scales are positively worded, higher directional preference estimates (which correspond with right-biased responding) will produce higher scale scores.

Hence, the observed positive correlation for the entirely positively-framed scale (motor impulsivity) and the negative relationship with the two reverse-scored BIS11 scales (attentional and non-planning impulsivity) are consistent with expectations about directional response styles.
Importantly, this also supports the inclusion of the directional preference parameter (where possible) as this kind of bias cannot be accounted for without it.

The directional preference parameter captures a tendency for individuals to preferentially select response options either above (right-biased) or below (left-biased) the middle of a scale.
However, the ability to estimate this parameter independently of latent state expression depends on survey design.

In the case of the BIS11, the structure of the instrument limits this separability, as its subscales do not intersperse positively and negatively worded items; instead, one subscale (motor) is positively keyed and the remaining two are fully reverse-coded.

Under these conditions, directional response tendencies cannot be mathematically disentangled from genuinely high or low latent state estimates, as both contribute to shifts in the location of the latent distribution.

Consistent with this constraint, the EFA results indicate that the factor capturing the BIS11 latent states (Factor 2) is also the factor which reflects the directional preference in a more evenly balanced scale (NEO).

In this paper, we have introduced a theoretical account of self-report that conceptualises responses as arising from two separable but concurrent sources of individual difference: the latent state(s) the task intends to measure and the respondent's decision process governing how those states are communicated.

By explicitly distinguishing between these components, the framework departs from traditional approaches that implicitly treat observed responses as direct reflections of underlying constructs, instead recognising that response generation also involves systematic, psychologically meaningful decision processes.

Importantly, the proposed framework does not privilege either source of information; rather, it treats latent states and response processes as equally central, and jointly they generate observed data.
We formalise this account for Likert-scale data using an ordinal-probit model and, in doing so, provide an interpretable account of how survey responses are generated.

The model defines three conceptually distinct psychological processes which combine to characterise response behaviour, reflected by mathematical transforms governing the spacing and location of response thresholds.
This quantifiable cognitive model represents a meaningful step toward a more psychologically grounded understanding of self-report responding.

It also has the potential to improve the precision and interpretability of latent state estimates by explicitly accounting for variability attributable to response processes, which is a long-recognised source of bias in self-report data (Baumgartner & Steenkamp, 2001; Paulhus & Vazire, 2007).

text.text: This theoretical perspective is not, in itself, novel or surprising.

The idea that self-reports are shaped by choices about how individuals disclose and convey information has long been acknowledged as a limitation of survey-based measurement (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007; Westland, 2022).

text.text: What we contribute is a quantitative, theoretically grounded framework for separating these two sources of information.
The LASARS model not only clarifies the nature of response behaviour but also generates novel, testable predictions about the interplay between response styles and latent state expression.
In doing so, it offers a new lens through which survey data can be interpreted more informatively.

The implications extend beyond the study of individual differences and response styles, providing value for any researcher or practitioner who relies on self-report measures to draw inferences about underlying psychological constructs.

Throughout this paper, we provide empirical support for the LASARS model's proposition that response style can be understood as a decision process under conscious control, while exhibiting a notable degree of stability across time and contexts when individuals choose their own response strategies.

This dual characterisation aligns with broader perspectives in the decision-making literature, which recognise that response strategies may reflect both situationally contingent processes (Ames, 2022; Heitz, 2014) and more enduring individual differences (D. R. Johnson et al., 2008; Wetzel & Carstensen, 2015).

text.text: We provide evidence that response styles and latent states are independent sources of variation and that, when this separation fails to occur, it is a consequence of poor scale design that confounds the two sources of information.

Importantly, our theory provides a principled solution to this confounding by allowing response style information obtained from well-designed external measures to be leveraged across tasks to mitigate the biasing influence of response style.

More specifically, our results indicate that relatively simple task instructions can induce systematic and targeted changes in response behaviour, particularly when respondents are asked to answer on behalf of another person.

Instructions designed to encourage more or less extreme responding produced predictable changes in the model's centre preference parameter, which is psychologically interpretable as reflecting extreme and midpoint responding.

Importantly, these shifts in response patterns were not accompanied by corresponding changes in latent state estimates, providing strong empirical support for the theoretical separation between substantive constructs and response processes.
In the absence of explicit instruction, we demonstrate that response style exhibits a high degree of temporal stability.

Consistent with prior work suggesting that response styles possess a stable, trait-like component over extended periods (Danner et al., 2015; Weijters et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2016; Wu, 2025), our findings show that response style is generally at least as stable as theoretically-related latent states over a three-month interval.

text.text: Hence, the persistence of response styles across measurement occasions suggests that they reflect enduring tendencies in how individuals engage with and use rating scales, rather than transient or purely situational decisions.
Similarly, we observed that response tendencies remained highly consistent across measures that differed in response format and theoretical framing.
Notably, response styles were generally as stable, and in many cases more stable, than the theoretically-related psychological constructs they accompanied.

This pattern aligns with prior research demonstrating that response styles generalise across tasks, instruments, and measurement contexts (Danner et al., 2015; Kieruj & Moors, 2013; Weijters et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2013), suggesting that they are not inherently tied to specific items, scales, or latent states.

text.text: At the same time, this finding stands in contrast to item-level models of responding, which have shown that extreme and midpoint responding may not remain stable when task features, such as the number of response categories, change (Ames, 2022).

text.text: Our proposed model helps reconcile these perspectives by demonstrating that, when response style is conceptualised broadly as a combination of multiple interacting response characteristics rather than isolated tendencies, it exhibits a high degree of cross-context stability.

In this sense, the proposed framework provides a more nuanced and integrative account of response behaviour, capturing consistent individual differences that extend beyond narrowly defined stylistic patterns and offering a clearer understanding of how response styles manifest across diverse measurement contexts.

Finally, we showed that poor scale design confounds the influence of directional response bias with latent state expression, and we tested a unique prediction derived from the LASARS framework: that response style information from one task can be used to compensate for design deficiencies in another, owing to the stability of response styles across contexts.

Consistent with this prediction, we demonstrated that the observed relationship between directional bias and latent state scores is substantially attenuated when information about directional bias obtained from a well-designed scale is incorporated into latent state estimation.
Importantly, this is not a prediction that purely statistical adjustment approaches can make.

Rather, it is only through the integration of a theoretical account with a formalised quantitative model that this hypothesis can be articulated, tested, and ultimately supported, highlighting the benefit of our proposed framework.
Taken together, these findings provide direct empirical support for the theoretical assumption that response style operates consistently across different latent states.
A key implication of these results is that further simplification may be both feasible and advantageous;
If response style is indeed stable across time and constructs, it may be reasonable to estimate a common set of response style parameters that generalise across measurement contexts.
This simplification provides a more parsimonious account of response style while retaining improved latent state measurement precision.

As we have demonstrated in Section 6, information about an individual's response behaviour obtained in one instrument can be leveraged to improve measurement precision in another, particularly in settings where direct estimation of response style is impractical due to suboptimal design or perhaps limited scale length.

For example, an organisation seeking to assess employee satisfaction using a brief five-item questionnaire may lack sufficient information to reliably estimate response styles within that instrument alone; however, if employees have previously completed a more comprehensive measure (e.g., a personality inventory during intake), response style parameters derived from that context could be incorporated to improve the accuracy and interpretability of the shorter satisfaction survey.

In this way, the theory supports a more integrated and cumulative approach to survey measurement, where response style is treated as a transferable source of information that can enhance inference across otherwise disparate data collections.

While previous research has established that response styles can exhibit consistency across time and tasks (Weijters et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2016; Wu, 2025), an important contribution of the present work lies in the model's ability to simultaneously estimate and directly compare response styles and latent states within a unified framework.

text.text: Given that our findings provide convergent evidence that response styles reflect systematic, domain-general tendencies in how individuals translate internal attitudes into observed responses, these processes should no longer be treated merely as nuisance variance to be controlled.

Moving beyond simplistic categorisations such as "extreme" or "acquiescent," the characterisation of more complex response style signatures may offer additional predictive utility, for example in explaining variability in behaviour or patterns of latent state expression.

Accordingly, the proposed modelling approach enhances the informational value of survey data by treating response style as an additional stream of signal, enabling richer inference and opening new avenues for understanding both how people respond and what their responses represent.

The LASARS framework also offers a new lens through which to interpret individual and group differences: are observed differences driven by true variation in latent states, or by systematic differences in how those states are communicated?

Prior research indicates that factors such as age, sex, and cultural background can influence response tendencies (Batchelor & Miao, 2016; Chen et al., 1995), raising the possibility that observed group differences may be partially confounded by response style.

Similarly, age-related changes in risk-taking (Duell et al., 2018; Rolison et al., 2014) and sensation seeking (Evans-Polce et al., 2018), which increase during adolescence and early adulthood before declining with age, closely mirror age-related variation in extreme responding (Batchelor & Miao, 2016).

text.text: This correspondence raises the possibility that some proportion of observed differences in self-reported risk-taking and sensation seeking as a function of age may reflect changes in response behaviour, rather than genuine differences in underlying latent states.
It is also possible that the same underlying psychological mechanisms that drive risk-related behaviours may also give rise to increased extreme responding.

In either case, our unified theoretical framework's ability to distinguish between latent state expression and response behaviour provides a principled means of disentangling these effects and advancing understanding of the complex relationship between substantive individual differences and their expression.

The LASARS model predicts that these known group differences in response style may be reduced through explicit instruction when these populations are being surveyed in much the same way that task instructions can change people's speed-accuracy tradeoff settings in speeded decision-making tasks (Larson & Hawkins, 2023).

text.text: This is an especially important consideration for use-cases where our proposed modelling solution cannot be appropriately applied, such as scales with only one latent state.

It should be noted, however, that the manipulation we demonstrate aimed to induce a specific response style and, while it is plausible that instruction may serve to reduce the inverse pattern (i.e., instructions which encourage midpoint responding may neutralise some extreme responding), concrete conclusions about how task instruction may be used to minimise known group differences in response style require further investigation.

Improving the precision of latent state measurement by reducing the potentially biasing influence of response style may also help to improve the poor correlations between self-reported and objective and behavioural measures of the same constructs.

Systematic reviews often conclude that correlations between self-report and behavioural measures fall within the weak to negligible range across many psychological domains, including inhibitory control (Saunders et al., 2018), self-regulation (Eisenberg et al., 2019), and emotional intelligence (Joseph & Newman, 2010).

text.text: However, isolating the potentially confounding influence of response styles from true latent state expression may enhance the predictive validity of self-report measures, leading to stronger and more consistent associations with alternative indicators of the same constructs.

In this way, self-report methods may regain some utility, as their considerable advantages -namely low cost, ease of administration, and straightforward analysis -are no longer undermined by systematic biases introduced by response styles.
It is important to note, however, that the present paper does not directly establish the model's ability to improve the construct or concurrent validity of survey instruments.

During model validation (see Supplementary Material), we demonstrate that the proposed model can recover known generating parameters, showing that it is capable of recovering ground truth when the data-generating process is aligned with the model.
However, evaluating whether this improves the ability of real-world survey instruments to recover an external ground truth lies beyond the scope of the present paper.

We have shown that the model can enhance convergent validity across multiple simultaneously administered surveys, but this does not include comparisons with gold-standard measures (i.e., concurrent validity), nor does it examine predictive validity.

Having established the theoretical validity of the framework and its capacity to disentangle response style from latent state information, an important avenue for future research is to quantify the extent to which the theory's bias reduction translates into gains in construct recovery, predictive performance, and overall measurement validity in applied settings.
It is also important to note that the LASARS model addresses systematic overuse or underuse of particular response options but does not extend to intentionally deceptive responding.

Although decisions about how to convey information that involve deliberate misrepresentation remain conceptually relevant, inasmuch as they still reflect choices about how information is communicated, they cannot be readily captured or disentangled within the present approach.
Deceptive responding effectively alters the latent state being expressed, meaning it cannot be identified as a response strategy that is separable from substantive latent states.
Accordingly, while the present framework distinguishes between two sources of variation in self-report behaviour, it does not provide a complete solution in all cases.

Just as the modelling approach cannot disentangle response style from latent states when poor scale design confounds the two, it is similarly limited when these components are intentionally conflated through deceptive responding.
Another general limitation of the current framing of response style is the lack of exploration of scales with more than five response options.

Although the LASARS model is mathematically generalisable to survey instruments with any number of response categories, the interpretation of the odds preference parameter would necessarily shift under these conditions.

The odds preference parameter, which reflects a tendency to select (e.g. 1-3-5) or avoid (e.g. 2-4) odd response options on a 5-point scale, would no longer map cleanly onto the same behavioural interpretation in scales with a larger number of categories.

For example, a high "odds preference" in a 6-point scale reflects high use of the first, third, fourth and sixth response options, changing the general interpretation and rendering the current parameter name misleading.

This limitation is somewhat mitigated by the fact that 5-point Likert scales remain the most widely used format in practice (Kusmaryono et al., 2022), suggesting that the current formulation retains strong practical relevance in many situations.

text.text: This paper makes two central contributions to the study and measurement of individual differences.

First, it advances a theoretical account of survey responding that treats response style as a psychologically meaningful and measurable source of individual difference, rather than unsystematic noise or a nuisance to be removed.
Second, it specifies a flexible model-based framework that operationalises this proposal, allowing latent psychological states and response styles to be estimated jointly.

By explicitly modelling response behaviour alongside latent state expression, the framework developed here offers a more complete representation of the processes that generate observed self-report responses than approaches that focus on either component in isolation.

This theory, and the findings presented in this paper which support it, challenge the conventional view that observed survey responses reflect latent states plus random error alone, instead positioning response style as a systematic, stable and informative source of individual differences that contributes meaningfully to observed responses.
Importantly, the LASARS model achieves these gains without requiring a priori identification or classification of specific response styles.

Instead, it estimates three-dimensional response style signatures directly from the data which, in turn, reflect a broad range of response tendencies, including complex or idiosyncratic patterns that are difficult to anticipate or label.
